claim: AURKA co-localises with the mitochondrial processing peptidase PMPCB in human MCF7 cell lines.
source: While exploring the localisation of AURKA at interphase, we observed that AURKA co-localises with the mitochondrial processing peptidase PMPCB in human MCF7 cell lines (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1A showing immunofluorescence data.

claim: The fluorescence signal of AURKA observed at mitochondria is specific, as it disappeared after AURKA knockdown by siRNA-mediated gene silencing.
source: The fluorescence signal of AURKA observed at mitochondria is specific, as it disappeared after AURKA knockdown by siRNA-mediated gene silencing (Figure 1A compare the two left panels and histograms).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of signal upon siRNA knockdown, referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: AURKA depletion leads to profound changes in the organisation of the mitochondrial network.
source: AURKA depletion also leads to profound changes in the organisation of the mitochondrial network, strongly suggesting a functional role of AURKA at mitochondria (Figure 1A compare the two middle panels).
evidence: The claim is based on observed morphological changes in mitochondria upon AURKA depletion, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AURKA localises to mitochondria regardless of the cell cycle phase and of its relative abundance.
source: In addition, AURKA localises to mitochondria regardless of the cell cycle phase and of its relative abundance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing AURKA at mitochondria across different cell cycle phases, referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AURKA can be detected as three isoforms: a predominant full-length isoform of ~46 kDa (AURKA46), an intermediate isoform of ~43 kDa (AURKA43), and a short isoform of ~38 kDa (AURKA38).
source: In immunoblots of total cell and mitochondrial lysates from HEK293 cells, AURKA could be detected as three isoforms: a predominant full-length isoform of ~46 kDa (AURKA46), an intermediate isoform of ~43 kDa (AURKA43) compatible with a first proteolytic cleavage by PMPCB (Chacinska et al., 2009), and a short isoform of ~38 kDa (AURKA38) that presumably represents the mature mitochondrial isoform and which is detectable with a monoclonal (Figure 1B) and a polyclonal anti-AURKA antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on western blot data showing three distinct AURKA bands, referenced in Figures 1B and 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AURKA43 is compatible with a first proteolytic cleavage by PMPCB.
source: In immunoblots of total cell and mitochondrial lysates from HEK293 cells, AURKA could be detected as three isoforms: a predominant full-length isoform of ~46 kDa (AURKA46), an intermediate isoform of ~43 kDa (AURKA43) compatible with a first proteolytic cleavage by PMPCB (Chacinska et al., 2009), and a short isoform of ~38 kDa (AURKA38) that presumably represents the mature mitochondrial isoform and which is detectable with a monoclonal (Figure 1B) and a polyclonal anti-AURKA antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the molecular weight of AURKA43 and knowledge of PMPCB cleavage, supported by citation to Chacinska et al., 2009.

claim: AURKA38 presumably represents the mature mitochondrial isoform.
source: In immunoblots of total cell and mitochondrial lysates from HEK293 cells, AURKA could be detected as three isoforms: a predominant full-length isoform of ~46 kDa (AURKA46), an intermediate isoform of ~43 kDa (AURKA43) compatible with a first proteolytic cleavage by PMPCB (Chacinska et al., 2009), and a short isoform of ~38 kDa (AURKA38) that presumably represents the mature mitochondrial isoform and which is detectable with a monoclonal (Figure 1B) and a polyclonal anti-AURKA antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the size and detection pattern of AURKA38 in mitochondrial fractions.

claim: Depletion of 80% of the mitochondrial protease PMPCB almost completely blocked the intra-mitochondrial cleavage of AURKA.
source: To confirm that AURKA43 and AURKA38 correspond to two AURKA isoforms processed inside mitochondria, we depleted 80% of the mitochondrial protease PMPCB. This almost completely blocked the intra-mitochondrial cleavage of AURKA (Figure 1C), strongly suggesting that AURKA43 and AURKA38 are mitochondrial cleavage products issued by PMPCB-related import pathways in the matrix.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced AURKA cleavage upon PMPCB knockdown, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AURKA43 and AURKA38 are mitochondrial cleavage products issued by PMPCB-related import pathways in the matrix.
source: To confirm that AURKA43 and AURKA38 correspond to two AURKA isoforms processed inside mitochondria, we depleted 80% of the mitochondrial protease PMPCB. This almost completely blocked the intra-mitochondrial cleavage of AURKA (Figure 1C), strongly suggesting that AURKA43 and AURKA38 are mitochondrial cleavage products issued by PMPCB-related import pathways in the matrix.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PMPCB knockdown experiment showing reduced cleavage, combined with knowledge of mitochondrial import pathways.

claim: Two semi-tryptic peptides starting at residues 33 and between residues 80–82 were retrieved, with sizes consistent with the molecular weights of AURKA43 and AURKA38, respectively.
source: We retrieved two semi-tryptic peptides starting at residues 33 and between residues 80–82; the size of these peptides was consistent with the molecular weights of AURKA43 and AURKA38, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data identifying specific cleavage sites, referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Ectopic AURKA fused to GFP is detected in the mitochondrial matrix and in contact with mitochondrial cristae.
source: We first detected ectopic AURKA fused to GFP in the mitochondrial matrix and in contact with mitochondrial cristae (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data showing AURKA-GFP localization, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AURKA is a soluble protein retrieved exclusively in the soluble fraction after sodium carbonate extraction.
source: To determine whether AURKA is a soluble protein or it is strongly attached to mitochondrial membranes, protein extraction with sodium carbonate was carried out on mitochondrial fractions of HEK293 cells (Figure 1E). AURKA was retrieved exclusively in the soluble fraction, reinforcing the conclusion that AURKA is mainly localised in the matrix as observed in TEM analyses.
evidence: The claim is based on biochemical fractionation data showing AURKA in the soluble fraction, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AURKA38 showed a degradation pattern similar to the matrix PMPCB protease in trypsin digestion experiments.
source: To further investigate the import of AURKA, we digested mitochondrial fractions of HEK293 cells with trypsin to eliminate mitochondrial protein precursors and peripheral Outer Mitochondrial Membrane (OMM) proteins, and we further combined trypsin with detergents to access the matrix. AURKA38 showed a degradation pattern similar to the one of the matrix PMPCB protease (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on protease protection assay data comparing AURKA38 and PMPCB degradation patterns, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: AURKA is localised to mitochondria at interphase and is imported and processed in the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Together, these data demonstrate for the first time that AURKA is localised to mitochondria at interphase and that it is imported and processed in the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: The claim summarizes multiple experimental findings including immunofluorescence, western blotting, and electron microscopy data.

claim: Decreases in donor fluorescence lifetime in FRET/FLIM analyses indicated physical proximity compatible with protein-protein interactions between exogenously expressed AURKA and all the major TOMM subunits, TOMM 20, 22, 40 and 70.
source: In this light, we searched for the physical proximity of AURKA with the subunits of the TOMM machinery by FRET/FLIM (Padilla-Parra and Tramier, 2012). Decreases in donor fluorescence lifetime in FRET/FLIM analyses indicated physical proximity compatible with protein-protein interactions between exogenously expressed AURKA and all the major TOMM subunits, TOMM 20, 22, 40 and 70 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing decreased donor lifetime, indicating proximity between AURKA and TOMM subunits, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The first 30 or 100 amino acids of AURKA fused to GFP were not detected in mitochondria by immunofluorescence microscopy or in mitochondrial fractions by western blotting.
source: The first 30 or 100 amino acids of AURKA fused to GFP were not detected in mitochondria by immunofluorescence microscopy, or in mitochondrial fractions of HEK293 cells subjected to western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is based on negative results from immunofluorescence and western blotting experiments, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The N-terminal of AURKA is not sufficient to shuttle GFP to mitochondria, suggesting the absence of a canonical MTS in these regions of the protein.
source: This indicates that the N-terminal of AURKA is not sufficient to shuttle GFP to mitochondria and it suggests the absence of a canonical MTS in these regions of the protein.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the negative results of N-terminal AURKA fragments failing to localize GFP to mitochondria.

claim: An AURKA truncation mutant in which the first 30 amino acids were removed (AURKA ΔNter) did not localise to mitochondria by confocal microscopy and western blotting.
source: However, an AURKA truncation mutant in which the first 30 amino acids were removed (AURKA ΔNter) did not localise to mitochondria by confocal microscopy and western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B) and did not interact with TOMM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), although catalytically active in vitro towards two AURKA substrates, histone H3 and RALA (Lim et al., 2010; Kashatus et al., 2011; Bertolin et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy and western blotting data showing absence of mitochondrial localization for AURKA ΔNter, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: AURKA ΔNter did not interact with TOMM.
source: However, an AURKA truncation mutant in which the first 30 amino acids were removed (AURKA ΔNter) did not localise to mitochondria by confocal microscopy and western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B) and did not interact with TOMM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), although catalytically active in vitro towards two AURKA substrates, histone H3 and RALA (Lim et al., 2010; Kashatus et al., 2011; Bertolin et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing no interaction between AURKA ΔNter and TOMM, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: AURKA ΔNter is catalytically active in vitro towards two AURKA substrates, histone H3 and RALA.
source: However, an AURKA truncation mutant in which the first 30 amino acids were removed (AURKA ΔNter) did not localise to mitochondria by confocal microscopy and western blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B) and did not interact with TOMM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), although catalytically active in vitro towards two AURKA substrates, histone H3 and RALA (Lim et al., 2010; Kashatus et al., 2011; Bertolin et al., 2016) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on in vitro kinase assay data showing AURKA ΔNter phosphorylates histone H3 and RALA, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, and supported by citations.

claim: The depletion of RALA does not inhibit the entry of AURKA into mitochondria.
source: We observed that the depletion of RALA does not inhibit the entry of AURKA into mitochondria. However, it impacts the abundance of AURKA to the same extent in total fractions and inside mitochondria. Therefore, the mitochondrial import of AURKA is RALA-independent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing AURKA in mitochondria after RALA depletion, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The mitochondrial import of AURKA is RALA-independent.
source: We observed that the depletion of RALA does not inhibit the entry of AURKA into mitochondria. However, it impacts the abundance of AURKA to the same extent in total fractions and inside mitochondria. Therefore, the mitochondrial import of AURKA is RALA-independent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RALA depletion does not prevent AURKA mitochondrial localization.

claim: AURKA38 was detected in cytosolic fractions of HEK293 cells, indicating that the kinase is exported from mitochondria after processing.
source: Intriguingly, AURKA38 was also detected in cytosolic fractions of HEK293 cells, indicating that the kinase is exported from mitochondria after processing (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing AURKA38 in cytosolic fractions, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MitoAURKA (AURKA with the first 30 amino acids replaced with a strong MTS from cytochrome c oxidase) was not exported back to the cytosol.
source: To establish whether this feature is intrinsic to the AURKA MTS, we replaced the first 30 amino acids of AURKA with a well characterised, strong MTS derived from cytochrome c oxidase, which is known to be recognised by TOMM and cleaved by PMPCB (Chacinska et al., 2009). This yields an exclusively mitochondrial AURKA (mitoAURKA), which was not exported back to the cytosol (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing mitoAURKA exclusively in mitochondrial fractions, shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3C.

claim: MitoAURKA did not localise at the centrosome when compared to normal AURKA.
source: In addition, mitoAURKA did not localise at the centrosome when compared to normal AURKA (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy data comparing centrosomal localization of AURKA and mitoAURKA, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The AURKA biosensor localises at mitochondria as endogenous AURKA in MCF7 cells does.
source: The AURKA biosensor localises at mitochondria as endogenous AURKA in MCF7 cells does (Figure 2D,E and see Figure 1A for comparison), and the decrease in the lifetime of GFP revealed that it is autophosphorylated on Thr288 and activated in mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is based on FLIM microscopy data showing the biosensor at mitochondria, shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: The AURKA biosensor is autophosphorylated on Thr288 and activated in mitochondria.
source: The AURKA biosensor localises at mitochondria as endogenous AURKA in MCF7 cells does (Figure 2D,E and see Figure 1A for comparison), and the decrease in the lifetime of GFP revealed that it is autophosphorylated on Thr288 and activated in mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing decreased GFP lifetime, indicating autophosphorylation and activation, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The activation of the AURKA biosensor in mitochondria is abolished by the AURKA inhibitor Alisertib (MLN8237).
source: This activation is abolished by the AURKA inhibitor Alisertib (MLN8237) (Figure 2D), an ATP-analogue currently under clinical trials (Görgün et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing no decrease in GFP lifetime upon MLN8237 treatment, shown in Figure 2D, and supported by citation.

claim: A kinase-dead mutant of AURKA (AURKA Lys162Met) was not retrieved in mitochondrial fractions.
source: In this light, we assessed whether a kinase-dead mutant of AURKA (AURKA Lys162Met) could shuttle to mitochondria. Indeed, AURKA Lys162Met was not retrieved in mitochondrial fractions (Figure 2F), indicating that the kinase activity of AURKA is required for its mitochondrial localisation.
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing absence of AURKA Lys162Met in mitochondrial fractions, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The kinase activity of AURKA is required for its mitochondrial localisation.
source: In this light, we assessed whether a kinase-dead mutant of AURKA (AURKA Lys162Met) could shuttle to mitochondria. Indeed, AURKA Lys162Met was not retrieved in mitochondrial fractions (Figure 2F), indicating that the kinase activity of AURKA is required for its mitochondrial localisation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that kinase-dead AURKA does not localize to mitochondria.

claim: Knockdown of AURKA led to mitochondrial elongation with swollen organelles showing intact cristae and no apparent loss of intramitochondrial content.
source: First, we analysed mitochondrial morphology by TEM in HEK293 cells. Knockdown of AURKA led to mitochondrial elongation: the organelles appeared swollen, but they showed intact cristae and no apparent loss of intramitochondrial content (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on transmission electron microscopy data showing mitochondrial morphology changes upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The silencing of AURKA increases the length of the whole mitochondrial network.
source: Analyses of mitochondrial length and branching (Koopman et al., 2005) revealed that the silencing of AURKA increases the length of the whole mitochondrial network (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), confirming previous results obtained with a kinase-dead version of AURKA (Kashatus et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial morphology, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When AURKA is over-expressed, mitochondria are interconnected and they pack into mitochondrial clusters.
source: Intriguingly, TEM analyses showed that mitochondria interconnectivity increases also when AURKA is over-expressed, again with no apparent signs of intramitochondrial content loss (Figure 3A). Under these conditions, analyses of mitochondrial network morphology showed that mitochondria are interconnected and they pack into mitochondrial clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on TEM and morphological analysis data showing mitochondrial clustering upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: AURKA loss-of-function mutants or those harbouring an AURKA-targeted RNAi and gain-of-function mutants (overexpression of Drosophila AURKA) showed more interconnected mitochondria than did controls in Drosophila.
source: AURKA loss-of-function mutants or those harbouring an AURKA-targeted RNAi and gain-of-function mutants (overexpression of Drosophila AURKA) showed more interconnected mitochondria than did controls (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C, red panels).
evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data in Drosophila showing increased mitochondrial connectivity, shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Mitochondria are interconnected in MCF7 cells both when AURKA is silenced or over-expressed.
source: By using the diffusion of red mitoDendra2, we confirmed that mitochondria are interconnected also in MCF7 cells both when AURKA is silenced or over-expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data in MCF7 cells, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mitochondrial interconnectivity in the presence of over-expressed AURKA depends on its capacity to be imported/exported, and on the kinase activity of AURKA itself.
source: We observed that mitochondrial interconnectivity in the presence of over-expressed AURKA depends on its capacity to be imported/exported, and on the kinase activity of AURKA itself, as the over-expression of AURKA ΔNter, mitoAURKA or the kinase-dead AURKA Lys162Met have no effect on mitochondrial elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data showing no effect on mitochondrial connectivity with AURKA mutants, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The role of AURKA in the regulation of mitochondrial morphology is conserved in flies and humans with no differences in mitochondrial connectivity due to the silencing or the overexpression of the kinase.
source: Therefore, the role of AURKA in the regulation of mitochondrial morphology is conserved in flies and humans with no differences in mitochondrial connectivity due to the silencing or the overexpression of the kinase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both AURKA knockdown and overexpression lead to increased mitochondrial connectivity in both flies and human cells.

claim: When AURKA was downregulated, the abundance of MFN1 and OPA1 increased while the level of DNM1L decreased.
source: When AURKA was downregulated, the abundance of MFN1 and OPA1 increased while the level of DNM1L decreased (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing changes in fusion and fission protein levels upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Downregulation of AURKA lead to an increase of Ser637 phosphorylation of DNM1L, corresponding to an increased cytosolic localisation of DNM1L.
source: We then analysed the phosphorylation state of DNM1L on Ser637, since DNM1L localises in the cytosol when phosphorylated on this residue and to mitochondrial when dephosphorylated (Kashatus et al., 2011; Wai and Langer, 2016). Downregulation of AURKA lead to an increase of Ser637 phosphorylation, corresponding to an increased cytosolic localisation of DNM1L (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing increased DNM1L Ser637 phosphorylation upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, and supported by citations.

claim: Increased mitochondrial connectivity at interphase could be reverted by normal AURKA expressed at physiological levels, but not by the cytosolic-only AURKA ΔNter.
source: Under these experimental conditions, increased mitochondrial connectivity at interphase could be reverted by normal AURKA expressed at physiological levels. On the contrary, the cytosolic-only AURKA ΔNter did not rescue mitochondrial elongation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), although this protein retains its catalytic activity and its capacity to phosphorylate RALA on Ser194 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on mitochondrial morphology analysis showing rescue by normal AURKA but not AURKA ΔNter, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: When AURKA was over-expressed, an increase of the short isoform of OPA1 (S-OPA1) was observed.
source: When AURKA was over-expressed, we observed the increase of the short isoform of OPA1 (S-OPA1), a phenomenon previously reported to be directly caused by an increased mitochondrial respiratory chain activity (Mishra et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing increased S-OPA1 upon AURKA overexpression, and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A small but significant decrease of the levels of DNM1L and its receptor MFF was observed when AURKA was over-expressed.
source: In addition, we also observed a small but significant decrease of the levels of DNM1L and its receptor MFF (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing decreased DNM1L and MFF levels upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Nearly 60% of cells with ectopic AURKA showed interconnected mitochondria clustered in the perinuclear region.
source: While analysing mitochondria in tumorigenic cells, we observed that nearly 60% of cells with ectopic AURKA showed interconnected mitochondria clustered in the perinuclear region (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial clustering in cells overexpressing AURKA, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F.

claim: AURKA-positive mitochondrial aggregates are SDS-insoluble as indicated by dot-blot filter retardation assays.
source: As mito-aggresomes, we found these AURKA-positive mitochondrial aggregates to be SDS-insoluble as indicated by dot-blot filter retardation assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: The claim is based on dot-blot filter retardation assay data showing SDS-insoluble AURKA aggregates, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G.

claim: The over-expression of the fly homologue of DNM1L – Drp1 – in flies over-expressing AURKA rescued mitochondrial interconnectivity.
source: In vivo, the over-expression of the fly homologue of DNM1L – Drp1 – in flies over-expressing AURKA rescued mitochondrial interconnectivity analysed with mitoDendra2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: The claim is based on mitoDendra2 photoconversion data in Drosophila showing rescue of mitochondrial connectivity by Drp1 overexpression, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3H.

claim: A direct interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF was retrieved by localised decrease of the lifetime of AURKA-GFP on mitochondria in FRET/FLIM analyses.
source: Furthermore, we retrieved a direct interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF by localised decrease of the lifetime of AURKA-GFP on mitochondria in FRET/FLIM analyses (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on FRET/FLIM data showing decreased GFP lifetime indicating proximity between AURKA and DNM1L/MFF, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF in the AURKA interactome was detected by nanoLC-ESI MS/MS.
source: Accordingly, the interaction between AURKA, DNM1L and MFF in the AURKA interactome was also detected by nanoLC-ESI MS/MS (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data identifying AURKA interactions with DNM1L and MFF, shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Over-expressed AURKA directly interacts with the fission proteins DNM1L and MFF and drives mitochondrial elongation.
source: Together, over-expressed AURKA directly interacts with the fission proteins DNM1L and MFF and drives mitochondrial elongation.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from FRET/FLIM and mass spectrometry data showing AURKA interactions with fission proteins.

claim: Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells show low expression levels of AURKA, whereas MDA-MB-468 and T47D express AURKA at higher levels.
source: Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells show low expression levels of AURKA, whereas MDA-MB-468 and T47D express AURKA at higher levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data comparing AURKA expression levels across four breast cancer cell lines, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mitochondria appeared more fragmented in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, and more elongated in MDA-MB-468 and T47D.
source: When looking at the morphology of the mitochondrial network, mitochondria appeared more fragmented in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, and more elongated in MDA-MB-468 and T47D (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy data showing mitochondrial morphology differences across cell lines, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MLN8237 had no effect on mitochondrial length in MDA-MB-468 and T47D cells, which express high levels of AURKA.
source: To correlate this phenotype with the abundance of AURKA, we inhibited the kinase with MLN8237. MLN8237 had no effect on mitochondrial length in MDA-MB-468 and T47D cells, which express high levels of AURKA and where the mitochondrial network is already dramatically interconnected per se.
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial morphology after MLN8237 treatment, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MLN8237 increased mitochondrial length and branching in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, where the abundance of AURKA is low and mitochondria appear fragmented in basal conditions.
source: Conversely, MLN8237 increased mitochondrial length and branching in Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells, where the abundance of AURKA is low and mitochondria appear fragmented in basal conditions (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of mitochondrial morphology after MLN8237 treatment, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AURKA plays two opposing functions in mitochondrial dynamics according to its abundance in the cell: contributing to organelle fission when expressed under physiological conditions, and directly increasing mitochondrial fusion when over-expressed.
source: Together, AURKA plays two opposing functions in mitochondrial dynamics according to its abundance in the cell: contributing to organelle fission when expressed under physiological conditions, and directly increasing mitochondrial fusion when over-expressed.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from multiple experiments showing different effects of AURKA on mitochondrial dynamics depending on expression level.

claim: These roles of AURKA are conserved in four carcinoma cell lines.
source: These roles of AURKA are conserved in four carcinoma cell lines, further increasing the relevance of these results.
evidence: The claim is based on data from four different breast cancer cell lines showing similar AURKA effects on mitochondrial morphology.

claim: The levels of the respiratory complex IV subunits increased in the presence of over-expressed AURKA.
source: Among the levels of steady-state respiratory complexes, western blotting analysis revealed that the levels of the respiratory complex IV subunits increased in the presence of over-expressed AURKA (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on western blotting data showing increased complex IV subunit levels upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increased abundance and activity of the respiratory complex IV are part of a mitochondrial-specific signature of epithelial cancers, which mainly rely on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production.
source: It has been reported that increased abundance and activity of the respiratory complex IV are part of a mitochondrial-specific signature of epithelial cancers, which mainly rely on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production (Whitaker-Menezes et al., 2011; Vyas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature about epithelial cancer metabolism.

claim: The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was increased when AURKA was over-expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: In this light, we observed that the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) – a measure of mitochondrial respiration – was increased when AURKA was over-expressed in HEK293 cells (Figure 5B) (Whitaker-Menezes et al., 2011; Vyas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on oxygen consumption measurements showing increased OCR upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The analysis of the interactome of AURKA by proteomics showed that AURKA directly interacts with multiple subunits of all respiratory complexes in HEK293 cells.
source: Although only the steady-state levels of complex IV increased significantly in the presence of ectopic AURKA, the analysis of the interactome of AURKA by proteomics showed that AURKA directly interacts with multiple subunits of all respiratory complexes in HEK293 cells (Supplementary file 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data identifying AURKA interactions with respiratory complex subunits, shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over-expressed AURKA globally acts on the mitochondrial respiratory chain to increase ATP production.
source: This reinforces the conclusion that over-expressed AURKA globally acts on the mitochondrial respiratory chain to increase ATP production.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of increased complex IV levels, increased OCR, and AURKA interactions with respiratory complex subunits.

claim: The over-expression of AURKA increased the proportion of cells exhibiting ongoing autophagy.
source: The over-expression of AURKA increased the proportion of cells exhibiting ongoing autophagy (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data measuring autophagy markers upon AURKA overexpression, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The downregulation of AURKA increased the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: On the contrary, the downregulation of AURKA increased the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Figure 5D), which has been proposed to be a complementary system of autophagy for the degradation of selective mitochondrial proteins (Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data measuring proteasome activity upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 5D, and supported by citation.

claim: Increasing levels of red mitoTimer were observed in cells transfected with an AURKA-shRNA, indicating that mitochondrial turnover was attenuated under these conditions.
source: To specifically evaluate the turnover of mitochondria, we calculated the red/green ratio of MitoTimer (Ferree et al., 2013). Increasing levels of red mitoTimer were observed in cells transfected with an AURKA-shRNA (Figure 5E), indicating that mitochondrial turnover was attenuated under these conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on MitoTimer fluorescence measurements showing increased red/green ratio upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 5E, and supported by citation.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ) measured with JC-1 or with TMRM decreased upon AURKA knockdown.
source: Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ) – another indicator of mitochondrial functionality – measured with JC-1 (Figure 5F) or with Tetramethylrhodamine Methyl Ester (TMRM) (Figure 5G) decreased upon AURKA knockdown, further confirming that mitochondria are defective in the absence of AURKA.
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data measuring mitochondrial membrane potential with JC-1 and TMRM upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: No global effect on the mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate was observed when AURKA was knocked down.
source: Although mitochondria are depolarised after AURKA knockdown, no global effect on the mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate was observed under these conditions (Figure 5H), despite both AURKA knockdown and over-expression have an impact on cell viability as previously published (Figure 5I) (Zhang et al., 2004; Bavetsias and Linardopoulos, 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on oxygen consumption measurements showing no change in OCR upon AURKA knockdown, shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The mitochondrial ATP production did not differ from that of control cells when AURKA was inhibited with MLN8237.

claim: AURKA maintains mitochondrial fission when expressed at physiological levels.

claim: Mitochondrial interconnectivity in the absence of AURKA is a consequence of a lack of fission.

claim: The absence of AURKA results in the mere accumulation of elongated mitochondria without any increase in the energetic capabilities of the mitochondrial network.
source: This results in the mere accumulation of elongated mitochondria without any increase in the energetic capabilities of the mitochondrial network.

claim: Over-expressed AURKA actively enhances ATP production by promoting mitochondrial interconnectivity.

claim: When AURKA is silenced, fission is inhibited.

claim: In conditions where AURKA is overexpressed, fusion is enhanced and so is the energetic capability of the entire mitochondrial network.
source: In conditions where AURKA is overexpressed, fusion is enhanced and so is the energetic capability of the entire mitochondrial network.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing increased S-OPA1, increased OCR, and increased ATP production upon AURKA overexpression.

claim: The simple interconnectivity of the mitochondrial network is not a direct readout of the energetic capabilities of mitochondria.
source: In conclusion, the modifications induced by AURKA to mitochondrial morphology are multifaceted and, in this context, the simple interconnectivity of the mitochondrial network is not a direct readout of the energetic capabilities of mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both AURKA knockdown and overexpression lead to interconnected mitochondria, but only overexpression increases ATP production.

claim: AURKA directly interacts with DNM1L and MFF.
